subject: health
unitTitle: Advocacy: Designing a Health Promotion Project
title: Guided practice: accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy
focus: accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy
essentialQuestion: What is the smallest change I could actually cause, and how would I know it worked?
keyPoints: Accurate advocacy distinguishes fact, estimate, and opinion, cites traceable sources, states uncertainty, and avoids promising outcomes the evidence cannot support.
A defensible advocacy product uses accurate evidence, a defined audience and responsible actor, a feasible request, privacy and access safeguards, and a measure for review.

For accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Design a complete health promotion project proposal — goal, audience, message, partners, constraints, and measurable outcome — for a setting the learner can actually reach. Execution is optional and guardian-approved; the proposal is what is assessed.
studentTask: Draft a one-page fictional advocacy component for accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy: state the goal with two facts, identify the audience and actor able to respond, propose one feasible action, add a privacy or access safeguard, and define one measure or critique question for revision.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
adaptationChoices: The proposal may be written, presented as a slide outline, spoken to an adult, or built on a supplied planning template. No public presentation or published material is required.
extensionChallenge: Apply accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy under a new constraint, compare two approaches, or explain the idea to someone else with an original fictional example, without completing another learner's graded work.
accessibilitySupports: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
The proposal may be written, presented as a slide outline, spoken to an adult, or built on a supplied planning template. No public presentation or published material is required.
trustedAdultNote: This course teaches health information and does not diagnose; direct urgent safety or health concerns to a trusted adult or qualified professional.

optionalReflection.prompt: Invite the learner to notice one safe, optional example of accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy in daily life. No purchase, account creation, photograph, recording, or private disclosure is required.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.

contentProvenance.objective: Explain accuracy, citation, and avoiding overclaim in advocacy accurately using current, reliable health information rather than assumption or anecdote.
